Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the simultaneously severe, poorly processed trauma-memory profile implied by 'Full Sensory Reliving' and 'Olfactory Recall'. Those latter items suggest intrusive sensory re-experiencing, while very easy verbal access points in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile in the same profile without additional context.

The Threat node is not coherent internally: 'Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating' is a non-threat/cognitive impairment item, whereas the other threat items are specific hypervigilant danger-monitoring states ('Waking Alert', 'Startle to Movement'). This makes the Threat selections thematically inconsistent.

Cross-node coherence is weak around 'Triggers: Being Followed'. That trigger implies a persecutory/social-tracking danger theme, but the rest of the profile centers more on restraint, safety checking, startle, and sensory reliving, without corresponding appraisals or memories about pursuit/tracking. It feels insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation.

'Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out' is not well linked to the selected trigger/threat pattern. The profile emphasizes tiredness, restraint sensations, night-time safety checking, and movement-related startle, but not a clear outside/public-space threat theme. Avoiding going out therefore appears mismatched to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Sophie is a 19-year-old dancer who came to treatment months after surviving a man-made disaster at a crowded performance venue where she had gone with other young dancers. What she can say about that night comes out in fragments. She knows what happened, but when she tries to put it into words she often stops, presses her hands over her face, and goes quiet, as if language disappears just as the scene returns in full. In her mind it does not feel like a story from the past. It arrives all at once, completely real, with the crush of bodies, the sensation of being pinned and unable to move, and the smell from that night coming back so vividly that for a moment she is back there rather than in the therapy room. What has stayed with her most sharply is the terror of being trapped in a crowd during an intentional act of human violence, feeling herself shoved, held, and unable to get free while people around her surged in panic.

In the weeks afterward, Sophie found that ordinary states of her body had become loaded with danger. When she was very tired after rehearsals, the heaviness in her limbs and the fogginess in her head felt too close to the helplessness she had felt that night. Exhaustion no longer meant she had worked hard; it meant she was vulnerable. She began watching for danger around her constantly. If someone moved suddenly near her, even another dancer crossing behind her in the studio, she reacted as if something terrible were about to happen. At night she woke abruptly and checked her room, listening and orienting herself until she could convince herself she was safe enough to lie back down. Even then, sleep stayed light and easily broken.

Being out in public became especially fraught. Walking to class or to the subway, Sophie often became certain someone was behind her or tracking her. She would glance over her shoulder repeatedly, change pace, or hold herself tense until she reached somewhere she could see an exit. In crowded sidewalks or hallways, if someone brushed past or a stranger came too close, her body reacted to the contact as though she were being restrained again. She sometimes lifted both hands to cover her face in those moments, partly to shut everything out and partly because she felt exposed and unbearably visible. The gesture had become automatic enough that she sometimes did it in the studio when other dancers noticed she had gone pale.

Before the disaster, dancing had been the place where Sophie felt most at home. Over time that changed in concrete ways. The studio mirrors, the physical closeness of partnering, and the fatigue after long rehearsals all became situations she dreaded rather than welcomed. She started declining invitations to go out with other company members after practice, then skipping nonessential outings altogether. On days when she did not absolutely have to leave home, she stayed in. She also gave up things she used to enjoy without quite announcing it to anyone: no more lingering after class, no more social evenings, no more pleasure in movement for its own sake. Friends saw less of her, and Sophie felt increasingly separate from other people her age. Watching classmates make plans and talk easily about performances, she had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere—not fully with dancers, not with carefree friends, not even with people who had known her before.

What troubles her deeply is not only that the disaster happened, but that it feels profoundly unfair and unresolved. She returns again and again to the fact that people did this, that the danger came from other human beings, and that “nothing has been done about it” is how it feels inside her when she thinks about the aftermath. At the same time, she tries hard not to think about it directly. She is frightened that if she lets herself remember on purpose, she will not be able to handle what comes back. So she organizes her life around not setting it off, even as reminders break through anyway in smell, touch, and sudden bodily states she cannot control.

By the time Sophie sought help, the strain was showing in every part of daily life. In rehearsal she struggled to concentrate on choreography and corrections, losing track midway through combinations she would once have learned quickly. She was sleeping badly, socializing less, and feeling increasingly alone. What finally brought her in was a recent moment in the studio when another dancer moved unexpectedly behind her and Sophie recoiled so violently that rehearsal had to stop. She was embarrassed afterward and shaken by how real the danger had felt. Sitting in treatment now, she is afraid that the memory will swallow her if she gets too close to it, and just as afraid that if nothing changes she will lose dancing, the one place she used to feel she belonged.
